policy_title: Restrict Junk Food Advertising and Extend Soft Drinks Levy
stated: Protecting children from exposure to junk food by supporting local authorities to restrict outdoor advertising and restricting TV advertising to post-watershed, and extending the soft drinks levy to juice-based and milk-based drinks that are high in added sugar.

source.quote: Protecting children from exposure to junk food by supporting local authorities to restrict outdoor advertising and restricting TV advertising to postwatershed. Extending the soft drinks levy to juice-based and milk-based drinks that are high in added sugar.

bearing_set.reason: Extending the soft drinks levy to juice-based and milk-based drinks directly raises prices on those products, affecting household food and drink costs, with a disproportionate impact on lower-income families who spend a higher share of income on such items.

Restricting junk food advertising and raising the levy on high-sugar drinks is a public health intervention aimed at reducing sugar consumption and obesity rates, which would plausibly reduce NHS demand for obesity-, diabetes- and dental-related treatment over time.

The levy extension generates new Exchequer revenue — the original soft-drinks levy raised ~£300–340m/year; extending coverage to additional product categories materially adds to that fiscal stream, affecting the funded/borrowed balance.

Consumption levies on food and drink are well-documented as regressive in direct incidence (lower-income households spend a higher share of income on the taxed goods), while any health benefits may be progressive (obesity rates are higher in deprived communities) — a genuine contested distributional effect on the rich–poor gap.

membership_note: Four fundamentals clear the non-negligible bar: healthcare (O3, primary mechanism), cost of living (O2, levy price pass-through), public finances (O12, revenue-raising), and inequality (O14, regressive incidence vs progressive health benefit). O10 (liberty) was considered but the advertising restriction bears on commercial entities not individuals, and the levy is a price nudge not a mandate — neither clears the bar. O11 was considered but the levy operates via product prices (O2's home) not income/take-home pay.
